title: Giving Devin your tools with MCP
subtitle: What it is, the four places it can run, and what each one costs you
footer: Synthetic reference system. No customer data, no real program.

slides.title: What MCP is, without the jargon
bullets: An MCP server is a small program that hands Devin extra tools: read a requirement, query the tracker, look inside a file
It answers three messages and nothing else: who are you, what tools do you have, run this tool
Devin either starts that program on your machine, or connects to one someone else hosts over HTTPS
The tools then appear in every session, named and described, instead of being re-explained each time
Hosting is only the question of where the program runs and who looks after it
slides.notes: Deliberately no protocol detail here. The three messages are initialize, tools/list, tools/call.

slides.title: What changes for the people doing the work
left: Every session starts by explaining the API again
Exports get pasted in by hand, or not at all
Each engineer improvises their own credential handling
No shared definition of what Devin is allowed to read
right: The tools are present at session start, already described
Each tool declares its inputs; bad arguments are refused
Credentials stay in the shell as placeholders, never in chat
One reviewed config entry the whole team clones

slides.title: MCP is one of four lanes. Use the cheapest that works.
rows: Repo files or a local stand-in
You have a token, want it simple
slides.note: Source: integrations/README.md. Transport and authentication are separate choices.
slides.notes: Point: MCP is not mandatory. Lane 1 needs no approval at all and is where a first visit should start.

slides.title: Where the server runs
slides.subtitle: Four honest answers, and what each one costs

slides.title: Pick one
slides.note: Source: integrations/mcp-hosting.md. Everything demonstrated in this repository is model A.
slides.notes: Do not let the room jump to C or D. The honest advice is A now, B when a second person clones, C when someone asks who audited the calls.

slides.title: Models A and B: run it on the laptop
left: Nothing leaves the machine; works with no network at all
No approval needed: it reads only what you can already read
Already set up here, one entry and one command
B adds a single reviewed entry that every clone inherits
right: Every laptop needs the runtime installed and kept current
No central record of who asked what
One credential per person to issue, rotate, and revoke
The server holds your permissions, so keep it read-only
slides.notes: B differs from A only in who owns the config entry. The secret still lives on each laptop.

slides.title: Model C: hosted by your platform team
left: One server, many laptops; nothing installed per machine
One audit log: tool, caller, time, outcome
One place to rotate or revoke a credential
Access controlled at the network and at the proxy
right: A real service to build, run, patch, and page on
A down host now stops everyone, not one person
Needs a TLS certificate the laptops already trust
Change control before the first user connects
Nothing in this repository stands one up for you
slides.notes: The reason to build C is the audit log. If nobody is asking for it, C is premature.

slides.title: Model D: hosted by the vendor
left: Nothing to host; the vendor runs and updates it
Browser sign-in gives per-user identity and expiry
Fastest path when the vendor already offers an endpoint
right: Requests leave your network for the vendor's cloud
A vendor outage or an expired token stops the tools
Needs administrator approval before the first connection
Do not assume it sits inside your authorization boundary
slides.notes: If the boundary answer is unknown, the correct action is to use the offline stand-in instead.

slides.title: Where the entry lives, and where the secret does not
bullets: Project file, checked in: the entry everyone who clones the repository should get
Local override, never checked in: your personal token, or something you are trying out
User file on your machine: servers you want in every project
Secrets are written as a placeholder that reads your shell or a file, never as the value
An override with the same name must repeat every key of the entry it replaces
A newly added server needs a new session; the list is read at startup

slides.title: The six questions Devin asks before writing any config
rows: Just you: A. Your team: B. Several teams, or one audit log: C.
Can this laptop reach the host?
Offline or unknown: A or B only. Internal host: C. Internet: D.
No or unknown: the entry is written disabled, or not at all.
A token in your shell, or single sign-on in the browser.
Which file should it go in?
Just you, everyone who clones, or every project on this machine.
If not, every write tool is named and approved one at a time.
slides.notes: This is the slide a security reviewer will care about most: no config is written until these are answered.

slides.title: What the readiness check enforces for you
bullets: Every entry in all three config files is validated, not just the one you edited
A remote server must use HTTPS, and a known transport
A local server's command must actually exist on this machine
Anything that looks like a pasted token is rejected outright
The wrong placeholder syntax is flagged before it silently becomes empty
An override that quietly drops a field fails the check
slides.note: Reproduce: python tools/doctor.py and python tools/check_repo.py; both report OK on a laptop with no network
slides.notes: Also worth saying: an unset variable becomes an empty string with no warning, which is why the check exists.

slides.title: What this repository has not proven
bullets: Model A is the only one tested end to end here
No hosted HTTP server, reverse proxy, or certificate is set up by this repository
No browser sign-in flow and no vendor endpoint has been exercised
Nothing here has been run inside a customer network or against a live tracker
File locations and CLI commands come from the product documentation; confirm them against your build
No vendor service is inside your authorization boundary by default
slides.note: Source: integrations/mcp-hosting.md, closing section; integrations/README.md, boundary reminder
slides.notes: Say this one out loud. It is the slide that makes the rest credible.

slides.title: What we need from you
bullets: Confirm the target: laptop now, and is a hosted server wanted later?
Name the first internal system worth exposing read-only
Tell us who approves a new internal host, and roughly how long that takes
Decide whether per-user identity must survive to the system behind the server
Provide a read-only token and a test project so we can prove the simplest lane first
slides.notes: Ask for a decision on the first two before leaving the room.

slides.text: Start on the laptop. Move to a hosted server the day someone asks who audited what Devin asked.
